analytic.title: A Low-Power Link Speed Control Method on Distributed Real-time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Distributed real-time systems that consist of multiple tasks with time constraints implemented on multiple processors have been used in various embedded systems, such as humanoid robots. These processors are interconnected with a real-time network, such as Responsive Link, in which data rate of each channel can be changed individually and dynamically. In this paper, we propose a low-power communication technique for distributed real-time systems. The power consumption is reduced by slowing down the data rate of communication link while satisfying the time constraints by exploiting the slack time, which is the difference between the arrival time of data and the deadline. We first measured power consumption of Responsive Link with various data rates and then implemented a real-time network simulator using the measured power values. We also implement a run-time communication mode change mechanism on Responsive Link and discuss the feasibility. Simulation results show that the proposed low-power packet transfer technique reduces the power consumption by up to 53.46% with a negligible degradation on the schedulability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Today, a large part of our life is supported by information system. Especially, real-time system such as automobiles and airplanes attracts huge social attention. In real-time systems, correctness of processing tasks depends not only on its result but also depends on time. Therefore, the system as a whole needs to meet time constraints while processing correctly. Since complicated systems such as humanoid robot has become quite widespread recently, new kinds of requisite features have appeared such as processing computationally hard tasks that require more than one processor and fault-tolerance of systems. In order to achieve these features, the demand on distributed real-time system is increasing. On distributed real-time systems, multiple distributed controller units are connected via real-time communication link and realize not only in-node realtime capability but also inter-nodes real-time capability.

There are a couple of communication standards that can guarantee real-time capabilities. For example, FlexRay [1], Time Triggered Ethernet (TTEthernet) [2] and Responsive Link [3]. These communication standards are appropriate for the applications such as control of automobiles and humanoid robots. Especially, in the application of embedded distributed real-time systems, low power consumption is also required in addition to real-time capability. Considering embedded applications powered by batteries and running on humanoid robots, which are commonly controlled by dozen of controller, low-power techniques are mandatory for both computation and communication system.

In this paper, we focus on power consumption on realtime communication link. We propose a technique to reduce power consumption while maintaining schedulability of each communication. Some prior researches have been conducted to reduce energy consumption of real-time communication. Luo [4] proposed an efficient scheduling algorithm that reduces energy consumption on embedded real-time system, in which supply voltage of processor and communication link can be adjusted. It efficiently schedule both processor and communication while keeping real-time constraint by Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS). In [5], authors proposed a historybased dynamic approach that expoloits communication link's utilization level as the load indicator of each router in NoC. It efficiently adjusts router voltage according to each router's load to reduce power consumption. In the experimental environment with a set of routers that support 4 level voltage modes, their approach achieved 3.3 times more power saving at maximum.

Responsive Link which is a communication standard for distributed real-time system, has a function to change communication speed dynamically. Since the speed of communication corresponds to the speed of controller LSI, energy consumption increases as communication speed becomes faster. In this paper, we focus on this functionality and propose a speed configuration method of communication link that exploits slacks. The proposed method reduces power consumption on distributed real-time systems by slowing down a communication speed based on the slack. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section explains the characteristics of our target communication link, Responsive Link. Section III proposes the low power packet transfer technique. In section IV, we first explain experimental measurement of energy consumption of Responsive Link and evaluate the proposed technique through simulation and discuss its performance. Finally, we conclude with a summary and future work in Section V.

div.head: II. DISTRIBUTED REAL-TIME COMMUNICATION STANDARD RESPONSIVE LINK
div.p: Responsive Link is a communication standard for distributed real-time system under development. It has been standardized as ISO/IEC 24740 [6]. Responsive Link is implemented on Responsive Multithreaded Processor (RMT Processor) [7] designed for processing tasks on distributed realtime system. In this section, we explain the characteristics of Responsive Link. formar requires strict time constraints and does not allow delay to deadline so that its data size is relatively small. The latter is more tolerant to delay, and requires larger bandwidth so that its data size is relatively larger. Taking humanoid robot for example, sending control packets corresponds to hard realtime communication because its data size is relatively small and delay is not allowed, and transferring pictures from camera corresponds to soft real-time communication because small delay is acceptable. There is a tradeoff between throughput and communication delay. Responsive Link provides communication lines that are physically separated to support both hard and soft real-time communication. Communication line for hard real-time communication is called Event Link, and the other one for soft real-time communication is called Data Link. In event-link, packet size is small 16 Bytes in order to shorten communication delay. On the one hand, data-link has larger 64 Bytes packet to increase throughput. As packet size increases, throughput increases. However, communication delay becomes longer at the same time. On the other hand, by reducing packet size, communication delay gets shorter while throughput decreases due to increased overhead.

div.head: B. Packet Overtaking
div.p: On Responsive Link, each packet has a 256-level priority, and priority based packet overtaking is implemented. Responsive Link has 4 ports for each node, each port is used as an input and output port to other nodes. When multiple packets from other nodes arrive at the same time, a conflict occurs. A packet with the highest priority will be sent first on a priority basis. By adopting priority based packet overtaking, the arrival time of packet can be predictable by Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) analysis. Therefore, schedulability of real-time communication can be guaranteed. In order to realize packet overtaking functionality, each node has priority arbiter and overtaking buffer. Also, it has a switch with external memory interface used to evacuate packets that overflowed from overtaking buffer. Each switch has five input and output ports. Port 0 is connected to the node itself leading to processor bus, and the other ports from 1 through 4 are used as an input and output port to other nodes. Packet overtaking can be seen as communication preemption, meaning that real-time scheduling theory for processor can be applied to communication.

div.head: C. Packet Routing Using Priority and Destination Address
div.p: Routing control is topology-free using routing table. Priority is used to route packets in addition to source and destination address. In this way, packets with the same source and destination address can take different routes. Therefore, it is possible to set up dedicated path and indirect route for high priority packets to avoid collision with other packets. Also, priority can be replaced on each hop to control each real-time communication in a distributed manner. By replacing priority, priority inheritance to lower priority packet and fine-grained flow control and speed control of packet become possible.

div.head: D. Codec and Communication Method
div.p: Responsive Link employes embedded clock serial communication [8]．Also, multiple error detection and correction code are employed to improve communication dependability. Appropriate code intensity and code rate can be selected as a function of given characteristic of transmission channel [9]. Three types of correction codes are supported: 8B10B Algorithm 1 Set Mode of Each Link for link id = 1 → num links do utilization = getU tilizationOf Link(link id) current mode = getCurrentM ode(link id) mode = getSlackAwareM ode(current mode, utilization) setLinkM ode(link id, mode) end for encoding [10], 4B10B encoding [9], and Non Return to Zero Inverted (NRZI) combined with Bit Stuffing (BS).

Modulation rate for each communication link is configurable to five levels of speed, 800, 400, 200, 100 and 50 [Mbaud], based on Digital Phase Lock Loop (DPLL) resolution performance. Each communication speed is called mode 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. Modulation rate can be set independently and dynamically for each port and each data and event link. In this paper, we focus on this functionality of Responsive Link. We propose a technique to reduce energy consumption by controlling communication speed while preserving real-time capability to the extent possible.

div.head: III. LOW POWER PACKET TRANSFER TECHNIQUE
div.p: In this section, we propose a packet transfer technique that reduces power consumption of a system, which is composed of dozens of point-to-point links, without damaging realtime capability to the extent possible.

div.head: A. Communication Mode Configuration for Each Link
div.p: We can set five levels of communication modes to each link. Mode 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. As experimental results shown in the next section suggest, as communication speed grows, power consumption increases. On the contrary, by slowing down the speed, power consumption can be reduced. Therefore, if the packet arrives at destination before the deadline, by exploiting the slack, which is the positive difference between the deadline and the arrival time, slowing down the modulation speed by setting communication mode appropriately makes it possible to reduce power consumption while meeting deadline constraints.

div.head: B. Communication Mode Configuration Exploiting Slacks
div.p: In order to slow down modulation rate of each communication link as possible as it can, it is useful to exploit the slack. If all communications in a network are single hop, it is possible to set communication speed as slow as possible by analyzing slacks. However, it is difficult to determine slack for each link on a hop-to-hop basis because slack of multi-hop communication is the time difference between arrival time and deadline to its end node that might be multiple hops away. Since low utilization of communication link implies larger slack, we assume utilization as important index of setting communication speed appropriately. If all the network flow (interval, source node, destination node, data size and route) is known beforehand, by analyzing all flows statically, we can calculate utilization of each communication link. As a function of this calculated utilization, it is possible to reduce power consumption in the system as a whole by setting mode for each link to the extent where real-time capability is preserved. Algorithm 2 is a pseudo code that returns newly set communication mode taking current communication mode and its utilization as inputs. Since we assume that, the lower the utilization is, the more we can set it slowly, Algorithm 2 slows down according to the utilization. Since the slowest communication speed on Responsive Link is mode 32, it is the slowest setting possible. For example, if the current mode is 4, if the utilization of that communication link is blow 50%, we set the communication mode 8 which has half the speed, and if it is below 25%, we set it mode 16 which is quarter of the current speed and so on.

div.head: IV. EVALUATIONS
div.p: In this section, we first measured power consumption of Responsive Link on prototyping. And we evaluate our proposed technique using the measured data to see how much power consumption can be reduced.

div.head: A. Power Consumption of Responsive Link
div.p: Before evaluating our proposed low-power packet transfer technique, we first evaluate the power consumption of Responsive Link to see its baseline power consumption. The measured real power consumption values are used for accurate power evaluation of the proposed technique later in this section. We implemented a simulator using data obtained from this experiment.

div.head: 1) Experimental Environment:
div.p: Responsive Link is implemented on RMT Processor System-on-Chip (SoC). We used evaluation kit which has RMT Processor System-in-Package (SiP) that has RMT Processor SoC, to conduct experimental energy measurement. Evaluation kit consists of main and sub substrates. 5V AC power is supplied via DC jack to the main substrate, and using on-substrate DC-DC converter to obtain lower voltage such as 3.3V and 2.5V to supply voltage with onboard various devices. RMT Processor is supplied with 1.0V which is generated by DC-DC converter converting supplied 3.3V. Running program boots from FPGA that is burned via JTAG. Fig. 1 shows our experimental environment based on the previous work [11] to measure power consumption. We measured current of electricity supplied to RMT Processor by using synchronized logic analyzer and oscilloscope. We set a rising edge of PIO monitored by logic analyzer as a common trigger. We used a logic analyzer of Agilent 16902A, and a oscilloscope of Agilent infiniium DSO 8040B. We removed 0Ω resistance where 1V family of electricity flows, and attached a short circuit loop and also extracted lead terminal tracks. We attached a current probe to the short circuit loop, and attached a voltage probe to the extracted lead terminal tracks. Under this environment, we measured electricity and voltage supplied to RMT Processor.

div.head: 2) Experimental Methodology:
div.p: We measured power consumption of Responsive Link under each active running modes and idle state. From the point PIO's rising edge, we collected 200k samples at a sampling rate of 1.0MSa/s. We selected 100k samples and calculated average values, omitting samples at both ends. Power consumption of Responsive Link is measured in both idle and active state. Data Link is used for this experiment. We measured power consumption in idle state in Fig. 2. Humanoid robot topology used in simulation relative way. We first measured power consumption when only Responsive Link module is active and other unnecessary modules being clock gated, and then subtract power consumption when all modules are clock gated from it. Next, we measured power consumption in active state using the program that clock gates all modules that are not necessary to use Responsive Link. By subtracting the result of the same program with Responsive Link clock gated, we obtained power consumption in active state for each communication mode.

3) Experimental Result: Table I shows power consumption of Responsive Link for each communication mode when only one link is activated. By calculating from the difference between the result in idle state, the increase for each communication mode when adding one more link activated is shown in the 4th row of Table I.
As the experimental results show, as a communication speed grows, a frequency and a power consumption grows. By using these obtained results, we evaluate our proposed technique by simulation.

div.head: B. Network Topologies
div.p: Three different network topologies are used in the sumulations. In each topology, all communication links are operated with full-duplex mode.
• Humanoid Robot Fig. 2 represents humanoid robot topology, composed of 17 nodes. This topology is inspired by Humanoid robot Kojiro [12].
• Mesh Topology This topology is composed of 4 by 4, 16 nodes.

div.head: • Random Topology
div.p: The number of nodes is 17. On each simulation trial, each node is randomly connected in a way that any node is accessible from any node.

div.head: C. Evaluation Methodology
div.p: By using experimental measurement results of power consumption, we implemented simulator written in Java and • Interval is randomly selected between 50 to 450 [μs].
The step for each interval is equal to 50.
• Deadline is set to be start time of the next interval.
• Sending data size is randomly selected between 2 to 18 [KBytes]. The step for each data size is equal to 2.
• Source and destination nodes are selected randomly.
• A minimal hop count path is selected.
• Packet priority is selected randomly from 0 to 255.
We simulated as a function of number of periodic messages above on the three topologies, we performed 100 trials for each combination. We obtained schedulability and power consumption as results.

div.head: D. Evaluation Results
div.p: Fig. 3,4,5 show schedulability for each network topology. The baseline means all communication link is set to be communication mode 2, the fastest configuration. In each trial, we simulated on exactly the same periodic message set for both baseline and proposed technique for each network topology.

We can see that for every topology, schedulability obtained from proposed technique is lower than that of the baseline. However, its difference is very small meaning that schedulability loss is negligible. Actually, the maximum difference for mesh topology was 0.82%, 0.81% for humanoid topology, and 1.39% for random topology. Therefore, the proposed technique can be applied to applications that have soft realtime communication, which is more tolerant to delays.

Next, for each topology, we simulated power consumption of a whole system of both baseline and proposed technique. Fig. 6 and7 show the reduction rate of power consumption. We evaluated the reduction rate of the whole power consumed in Responsive Link network, and dynamic part of the reduction rate which changes configuring communication speed of each link. Fig. 6 shows how much power has been reduced compared to the baseline by using the proposed technique.

We can see from Fig. 6 that the algorithm achieved maximum reduction rate of 11.45% for humanoid robot topology, 13.09% for mesh topology and 8.29% for random topology. Fig. 7 shows reduction rate of dynamic energy consumption fluctuating by the setting of Responsive Link modes. We can see from Fig. 7 that the algorithm achieved maximum reduction rate of 52.39% for humanoid robot topology, 53.46% for mesh topology and 49.02% for random topology.

We can see that as the average data transfer rate in the system increases, reduction rate of power consumption becomes lower. This is because as the transferring data in the system increases as the number of generating messages grows, the utilization for each link get higher so that the slack, the difference between the deadline and the arrival time, becomes smaller. It can be said that our proposed technique is useful

div.head: E. Mode Change Latency
div.p: In this section, the latency overhead for the proposed speed control method is evaluated, since it affects the gain of mode changes. A run-time communication speed control procedure shown in Fig. 8 is implemented on Responsive Link. In this procedure, node 0 first sends a request packet of speed control, and then node 1 sends an acknowledge packet of speed control. Both nodes configure the digital phase lock loop to change the link speed. After that, node 0 sends an request packet of resynchronization, and node 1 sends an acknowledge packet of re-synchronization. Lastly, both nodes send an initialization packet to each other. We measure the turnaround time of the speed control sequence by cycle-level simulation using Verilog HDL. We used an Event Link for communication of the speed control procedure, and Data link is the controlled link. This procedure can be implemented on Responsive Link, since the communication lines are physically separated into Event Link and Data Link. We measure the latency overhead under following conditions to show the worst case response time.
• A cache system is disabled.
In the worst case, every memory access (instruction fetch and load store operations) introduces a cache miss.
• Packet data are transferred with a DMA (Direct Memory Access) controller.
To estimate a precise overhead, a program must be optimized.

The latency overhead for the run-time speed control procedure is 49,460 ns. In real-time systems, it is necessary to estimate the gain and overheads to reduce the power consumption while guaranteeing the time constraints, since the latency overhead may introduce the deadline misses. We are currently developing a run-time communication speed assignment algorithm that takes into account the overheads to further improve the power and performance efficiency.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a technique to set Responsive Link communication speed mode appropriately assuming lower utilization of communication implies larger slack generated when packet arrival time is earlier then the deadline. Also, we measured the power consumption of Responsive Link, and obtained energy consumption data for each mode setting of Responsive Link. By using the results, we implemented a simulator written in Java. We built a simulation environment of a real-time system using Responsive Link to evaluate the power consumption. Given randomly generated periodic message set, the simulation results show that our proposed slack-aware technique reduced the power consumption by up to 53.46% with a negligible degradation on the schedulability. The proposed technique is applicable for distributed soft realtime systems that allows certain amount of delay to deadline. Especially, this technique is useful for systems that require low power consumption such as humanoid robots that are driven by a battery.

Lastly, we implemented a run-time communication mode change mechanism on Responsive Link and showed that the latency overhead for the run-time speed control procedure is 49,460 ns. As a future work, we are extending this work so as to support dynamic communication mode change at runtime taking speed transition overhead into account to further improve the power and performance efficiency.
